verses.zh: （大卫的诗，交与伶长耶杜顿。）我曾说：我要谨慎我的言行，免得我舌头犯罪；恶人在我面前的时候，我要用嚼环勒住我的口。
verses.en: For the music director, Jeduthun; a psalm of David.I decided,[NOTE:1] “I will watch what I sayand make sure I do not sin with my tongue.[NOTE:2] I will put a muzzle over my mouthwhile in the presence of an evil person.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Psalm 39. The psalmist laments his frailty and mortality as he begs the Lord to take pity on him and remove his disciplinary hand.
Heb “I said.”
Heb “I will watch my ways, from sinning with my tongue.”

verses.zh: 我默然无声，连好话也不出口；我的愁苦就发动了，
verses.en: I was stone silent;[NOTE:1] I held back the urge to speak.[NOTE:2] My frustration grew;[NOTE:3]
notes: The psalmist wanted to voice a lament to the Lord (see vv. 4-6), but he hesitated to do so in the presence of evil people, for such words might be sinful if they gave the wicked an occasion to insult God. See C. A. Briggs and E. G. Briggs, Psalms (ICC), 1:345.
Heb “I was mute [with] silence.”

Heb “I was quiet from good.” He kept quiet, resisting the urge to find emotional release and satisfaction by voicing his lament.sn I held back the urge to speak. For a helpful discussion of the relationship (and tension) between silence and complaint in ancient Israelite lamentation, see E. S. Gerstenberger, Psalms, Part I (FOTL), 166-67.

verses.zh: 我的心在我里面发热。我默想的时候，火就烧起，我便用舌头说话。
verses.en: my anxiety intensified.[NOTE:1] As I thought about it, I became impatient.[NOTE:2] Finally I spoke these words:[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “and my pain was stirred up.” Emotional pain is in view here.
Heb “my heart was hot within me.”
Heb “In my reflection fire burned.” The prefixed verbal form is either a preterite (past tense) or an imperfect being used in a past progressive or customary sense (“fire was burning”).

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你叫我晓得我身之终！我的寿数几何？叫我知道我的生命不长！
verses.en: “O Lord, help me understand my mortalityand the brevity of life.[NOTE:1] Let me realize how quickly my life will pass.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “I spoke with my tongue.” The phrase “these words” is supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.
Heb “Cause me to know, O Lord, my end; and the measure of my days, what it is!”

verses.zh: 你使我的年日窄如手掌；我一生的年数，在你面前如同无有。各人最稳妥的时候，真是全然虚幻。（细拉）
verses.en: Look, you make my days short lived,[NOTE:1] and my life span is nothing from your perspective.[NOTE:2] Surely all people, even those who seem secure, are nothing but vapor.[NOTE:3] (Selah)
notes: Heb “Let me know how transient I am.”

Heb “Look, handbreadths you make my days.” The “handbreadth” (equivalent to the width of four fingers) was one of the smallest measures used by ancient Israelites. See P. C. Craigie, Psalms 1-50 (WBC), 309.
Heb “is like nothing before you.”

verses.zh: 世人行动实系幻影。他们忙乱，真是枉然；积蓄财宝，不知将来有谁收取。
verses.en: Surely people go through life as mere ghosts.[NOTE:1] Surely they accumulate worthless wealthwithout knowing who will eventually haul it away.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “surely, all vapor [is] all mankind, standing firm.” Another option is to translate, “Surely, all mankind, though seemingly secure, is nothing but a vapor.”

Heb “surely, as an image man walks about.” The preposition prefixed to “image” indicates identity here.sn People go through life (Heb “man walks about”). “Walking” is here used as a metaphor for living. The point is that human beings are here today, gone tomorrow. They have no lasting substance and are comparable to mere images or ghosts.

verses.zh: 主啊，如今我等甚么呢？我的指望在乎你！
verses.en: But now, O Lord, upon what am I relying?You are my only hope![NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “Surely [in] vain they strive, he accumulates and does not know who gathers them.” The MT as it stands is syntactically awkward. The verb forms switch from singular (“walks about”) to plural (“they strive”) and then back to singular (“accumulates and does not know”), even though the subject (generic “man”) remains the same. Furthermore there is no object for the verb “accumulates” and no plural antecedent for the plural pronoun (“them”) attached to “gathers.” These problems can be removed if one emends the text from הֶבֶל יֶהֱמָיוּן (hevel yehemayun, “[in] vain they strive”) to הֶבְלֵי הָמוֹן (hevle hamon, “vain things of wealth”). The present translation follows this emendation.

verses.zh: 求你救我脱离一切的过犯，不要使我受愚顽人的羞辱。
verses.en: Deliver me from all my sins of rebellion.Do not make me the object of fools’ insults.

verses.zh: 因我所遭遇的是出于你，我就默然不语。
verses.en: I am silent and cannot open my mouthbecause of what you have done.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “my hope, for you it [is].”

verses.zh: 求你把你的责罚从我身上免去；因你手的责打，我便消灭。
verses.en: Please stop wounding me.[NOTE:1] You have almost beaten me to death.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “because you acted.” The psalmist has in mind God’s disciplinary measures (see vv. 10-13).
Heb “remove from upon me your wound.”

verses.zh: 你因人的罪恶惩罚他的时候，叫他的笑容（的笑容：或译所喜爱的）消灭，如衣被虫所咬。世人真是虚幻！（细拉）
verses.en: You severely discipline people for their sins;[NOTE:1] like a moth you slowly devour their strength.[NOTE:2] Surely all people are a mere vapor. (Selah)
notes: Heb “from the hostility of your hand I have come to an end.”
“with punishments on account of sin you discipline a man.”

verses.zh: 耶和华啊，求你听我的祷告，留心听我的呼求！我流泪，求你不要静默无声！因为我在你面前是客旅，是寄居的，像我列祖一般。
verses.en: Hear my prayer, O Lord.Listen to my cry for help.Do not ignore my sobbing.[NOTE:1] For I am a resident foreigner with you,a temporary settler,[NOTE:2] just as all my ancestors were.
notes: Heb “you cause to dissolve, like a moth, his desired [thing].” The translation assumes an emendation of חֲמוּדוֹ (khamudo, “his desirable [thing]”) to חֶמְדוֹ (khemdo, “his loveliness” [or “beauty”]), a reading that is supported by a few medieval Hebrew mss.
Heb “do not be deaf to my tears.”

verses.zh: 求你宽容我，使我在去而不返之先可以力量复原。
verses.en: Turn your angry gaze away from me, so I can be happybefore I pass away.[NOTE:1]
notes: The Hebrew terms גֵּר (ger, “resident foreigner”) and תּוֹשָׁב (toshav, “resident/dweller”) have similar meanings. They are not used here with the technical distinctions of most references in Mosaic Law. Ps 39:12 takes up this language from Lev 25:23 where the terms emphasize that Israel would be a guest on God’s land. They were attached to the Lord’s household; they did not own the land. The Psalmist identifies himself with this privileged yet dependent position. Abraham also refers to himself by these terms in Gen 23:4.
